item.title: Chest
item.description: This chest was fun to create, as it is pretty self explanatory. I got to learn more about how to correctly use loop cuts to create an added level of detail. This was the first Blender project that I got to use my graphics tablet for. I got to play around with different brush sizes and layering colours. I feel like I could’ve improved upon the corner pieces. When painting on top of them, I noticed that the paint was jagged.

item.title: Fish
item.description:
I created this fish before I had a graphics tablet, so sculpting the features with a mouse was quite difficult. With this also being my first attempt at sculpting anything, I was just shooting in the dark. I am pleased with how it came out, with my main pride being the shape of the body and, at the time, the eyes. I had decided that I would give it another try when I had a graphics tablet to compare.

With a graphics tablet, and a little more time on Blender, my second attempt at sculpting a fish was much better. The scales, fins, and mouth are a lot more defined and “fish-like”. I also learnt the importance of different sizes of sculpting tools, and how to add intricate detail. I also wanted to focus on mixing some colours on the fish to make it pop more.

item.title: Weapons
item.description: This was fairly simple to create, as the main blade only required a plane. I used a reference image of a sword and traced the outline with a plane. I then extruded it and added faces, allowing for a more solid look. The hilt required a cube to be scaled and extruded to fit to size. I struggled a little bit with trying to extrude the faces of the blade’s plane out, as some of the faces weren’t selecting. But I just re-did the blade, which solved that.

item.title: My Drawings
Clay Girl
item.description: This was my first time creating a human character in Blender, and my first time designing hair. This character was fairly simple, with extruding objects and moving vertices being the main focus. I got to explore the mirror modifier, and understand how that works in relation to where an objects point of origin is placed. I would like to attempt to rig this character, so I can give it a walk cycle. At a later date, I would also like to try and add more detail to the face to actually give it some features.

item.title: Donuts!!!
item.description:
Add shape-Mesh-Torus

Right click- Shade Smooth

Modifiers- Add Modifier- Generate- Subdivision Surface

Hit TAB to enter Edit Mode, click on point, tap “G” and drag mouse using scroll wheel to give object more natural shape.

Click on point in the center, hold ALT and click on a center edge, press “S” to scale the middle part down slightly.

With the main donut selected, press Shift+D to duplicate the object. Right click to keep the new mesh in the same place. Name this new mesh to “Icing”. With the icing selected, go to edit mode and click the Toggle X-ray button. Select all the middle vertices around the donut and hit the delete key, clicking “Vertices”.

Go to properties on the icing. Click Generate- Solidify. Drag “Offset” all the way to 1.

Enable snapping. deselect Increment. Select Face Project. Turn off Proportional Editing, enable the Subdivision property to increase number of faces. Now, you can select vertex, press “G” and drag up or down (Using scroll wheel), to create an icing dripping effect.

With icing selected, add another Subdivision Modifier.

Enter edit mode, select two vertices, hit “E” to extrude, left click. Repeat 3 times for one icing drip.

With Icing selected, go to the modifiers page and add a new modifier. Deform- ShrinkWrap. Use the eye dropper tool next to the modifier and select the donut. Then move the ShrinkWrap modifier to the top of the modifier stack, as it needs to be done before the solidify modifier. Apply the solidify modifier on the icing.

Enter Sculpt mode and select the Inflate tool. Adjust the brush size and strength of your tool and then sculpt the endings of the icing. This creates a more natural “pooling” effect for the icing.

Hit the “M” key to enter the mask tool mode. Adjust brush size and set strength to 1. Apply the mask to the low points of your icing, trying to keep it as even as possible, avoiding the icing drips. Shift+I to invert the mask.

Use the filter brush to create an “icing rim” around the donut. Once, happy with size, remove the mask. Select the smooth tool to smooth out some areas that may be too thick or messy.

With Icing selected, go to the materials tab and create a new material. Change the colour to pink and turn the roughness down to about 0.2/0.3.

Do the same for the donut. Choosing an orangey/yellow colour.

Select Icing. Shift+click Donut body. Ctrl+P and click Object (Keep Transform), to parent the Donut and Icing together.

Add mesh- Plane. To add counter top.

Add new material on the plane. Base Colour- Image texture.

Apply a marble image to the material.

Enter the Shading tab at the top of the screen to open up the nodes area. Add a new node to change the roughness of the marble. This is to give it more texture.

These are the nodes and settings needed to add sufficient texture to the marble counter top.

Enter Texture Paint mode at the top of the screen. “/” to isolate the donut base when it is selected. Ass new material, add Image Texture. Edit this to the same colour as the donut base as before.

Paint in a slightly lighter colour around the donut to make it appear more natural.

Enter the Geometry Node tab a the top of the screen and with the icing selected, hit “New Geometry Node”. Add a node that says “Distribute Points on Faces” and connect it to a new node called “Join Geometry”. Don’t forget to also join “Group Input: Geometry” to “Join Geometry: Geometry”. This ensures that you can have both the points on face (sprinkles) and keep the icing mesh.

Shift+A-Mesh-UV Sphere to add a sprinkle shape.

Drag and drop the UV Sphere information into the Geometry Nodes section. This translates all the data into the “Object Info” node. Add “Instances on Points” node, and connect “Object Info: Geometry” to “Instances on Points: Instances”.

Enter Weight Paint mode and paint where you want sprinkles to be.

In Geometry Nodes, add new node called “Names Attribute”. Attach “Distribute Points on Face: Density Factor” to “Named Attribute: Attribute”.

Scale the donut, sprinkle and counter down to 0.1m. You may run into some issues with the sprinkles at this point. My sprinkles became tiny. If this happens, select sprinkle, press “S” to scale it up in size, CTRL+A to apply scale changes.

To start making long sprinkles, add a cylinder mesh and scale it down to the smallest value it can go.

Select the top and bottom face and CTRL+B to bevel the faces to appear more rounded.

SHIFT+D to duplicate. Enter Wireframe mode, highlight the top of the sprinkle and press G+Z to elongate. Repeat process 3 times. With the last sprinkle, CTRL+R to add loop cuts. Go to the modifier stack and add a Simple Deform Modifier, ensuring you switch the mode to “Bend”.

Drag and drop all 4 Sprinkle information into Geometry Nodes And attach “Collection Info- Instances” to “Instance on Points- Instance”. Add “Rotate Rotation” node and switch it to Local. Assign a random value to the rotation node.

This is what the second donut should look like after playing around in Geometry Nodes.

Select all of the sprinkles (including the round sprinkle) and link them all together. Create a new material on the bent sprinkle to do this.

With the bent sprinkle selected, go to the shading tab. SHIFT+A to add an Object Info Modifier. SHIFT+A again to add Colour Ramp modifier. Join “Colour” to “Base Colour”. With Colour Ramp, you can select whatever colours you wish your sprinkles to be and adjust the sliders to vary the proportion of these colours on the donuts.

Place camera and Light in desired places and click “Rendered Viewport”. You may have to change “Render through CPU” to “Render through GPU”.

SHIFT+A- mesh- circle to give a foundation to the plate. From here, you have to extrude and shade-smooth until you have a shape that you are happy with.

Duplicate the marble countertop and position it behind the original to create a “splashback” for the scene.

Duplicate and position the donuts for the scene. Here, you can change the colour of the icing and decide which donuts you want to have certain sprinkles. The colour of the icing can be changes in the materials window on the selected donut.

Delete the “Light” object that is already in the scene. Selecting the World window on the left hand side, change the “Colour” to “Sky Texture”. This will create a dynamic “Sun” in our scene that we can edit the properties of. I wanted to go for a natural evening glow for my scene, so these are the changes in Elevation and Sun Rotation that I made.

This is what the first render looks like. From here, I can go back and add more objects to create a scene, I could tweak some colours, focus on shadows.

item.title: Starting My Journey
item.description:
Starting My Journey

Welcome to my digital playground! My name is Kez, and I’m thrilled to share my journey into the fascinating world of game design. This is a zero-to-hero adventure, as I start with no prior experience in the art of game design/development.

About Me

I’ve always been captivated by the magic of video games—the mesmerizing visual effects (VFX), the immersive music, and the stunning scenery that games showcase. These elements create an atmosphere that transports players to different worlds, and I aspire to be a part of crafting such experiences.

Learning Path

To embark on this journey, I’m leveraging resources like Udemy and YouTube, which offer a wealth of tutorials and courses on game design and development. These platforms have been invaluable in providing me with the foundational knowledge I need to get started.

Tools and Languages

I’m currently focused on mastering two powerful game engines: Unity and Unreal Engine.

  • Unity: In Unity, I’m learning C#, a versatile programming language that allows me to create complex game mechanics and interactive experiences.

  • Unreal Engine: With Unreal Engine, I’m diving into C++, a robust language that offers deep control over game systems and performance.

My Passion

Visual effects (VFX) are my favorite aspect of games. The way VFX can transform a simple action into an awe-inspiring spectacle is truly magical. Additionally, I have a deep appreciation for the music and scenery in games. These elements not only enhance the visual appeal but also build the overall atmosphere, making the gaming experience memorable.

Aspirations

My ultimate goal is to work for a renowned game development studio such as Naughty Dog or Sucker Punch. These companies are known for their ground-breaking games and innovative approaches to storytelling and gameplay. Being a part of such a team would be a dream come true, allowing me to contribute to the creation of extraordinary gaming experiences.

Conclusion

This journey is just beginning, and I invite you to join me as I navigate the challenges and triumphs of learning game design. I’ll be sharing my progress, insights, and the projects I work on along the way. Let’s explore the intricacies of technology and game design together and watch as this zero-to-hero story unfolds.
